name: Oil pulling

card.summary: Swishing coconut or sesame oil, an Ayurvedic practice with small trials on gum health and no solid evidence for whitening.
card.note: Case reports of lipoid pneumonia from aspirated oil; ADA says no reliable studies support it.

quick.overview:
Oil pulling is the practice of swishing an edible oil, such as sesame or coconut oil, around the mouth for a period and then spitting it out. It comes from Ayurvedic tradition and has been promoted in recent years for oral hygiene, bad breath, gum health and whiter teeth.

Small trials have looked at plaque, gingivitis and bacterial counts, with mixed results. In looksmaxxing forums it is debated mainly as a whitening method, for which no study was identified.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say oil 'pulls' bacteria and toxins from the mouth. A skeptic commentator cited on Wikipedia suggests any benefit is from mechanical swishing. Some oils contain compounds, such as lauric acid in coconut oil, that have been proposed to be antimicrobial.
quick.risks: Dental bodies describe it as unlikely to harm, though the American Dental Association says no reliable studies support it. Case reports describe exogenous lipoid pneumonia after repeated sesame oil pulling, and it is not recommended for young children because of swallowing risks.

lead: Oil pulling is a traditional practice from Ayurvedic medicine in which an edible oil, commonly sesame, coconut or sunflower, is swished around the mouth for several minutes and then spat out, much like a mouthwash.[1] Ayurvedic texts refer to it as kavala or gandusha, and it is promoted for oral hygiene, fresher breath, gum health and, in modern wellness circles, whiter and cleaner-looking teeth.[2][3] For people who care about their smile, the appeal is a cheap, food-grade routine that they hope will keep plaque and stain down and breath fresh, which are two things that shape how teeth and the lower face present.

Clinical research consists mostly of small trials and reviews from the 2000s onward. Several randomized trials report reduced plaque, gingivitis or bacterial counts compared with controls, while meta-analyses report salivary bacterial-count reductions with mixed results for plaque and gingival indices.[10][11][12][14][15] A 2016 systematic review found the trials few and underpowered, and the American Dental Association says there are no reliable studies supporting the practice for oral hygiene or wellbeing.[1] No trial has measured tooth whitening as an outcome.[22]

Case reports describe lipoid pneumonia after aspiration of oil during repeated pulling.[5] In looksmaxxing communities oil pulling is discussed mainly as a low-cost whitening and breath habit, often compared with hydrogen peroxide strips and professional whitening.[6][7]

paras: Oil pulling involves taking an edible oil into the mouth, moving it around the teeth and gums as though rinsing, and spitting it out rather than swallowing.[1] Wikipedia's tooth-whitening article lists it among home remedies as an Ayurvedic practice using coconut or olive oil swished for up to 20 minutes daily.[22]
Oils used include sesame, the traditional choice in Ayurveda, plus coconut, sunflower and olive oil or herbal oils.[1][2] Coconut oil is roughly half lauric acid, a medium-chain fatty acid.[23]

Oil pulling is described in the Ayurvedic tradition as a daily hygiene practice, together with tongue scraping and tooth cleaning (dinacharya).[24][2] Ayurveda, the traditional medicine system of the Indian subcontinent, took its classical texts to their present form in the early centuries CE; modern scientific reviewers describe its theory as unsupported by evidence.[24]

A reference summary credits the Ukrainian physician F. Karach with presenting oil pulling at a conference in 1992 and with a modern revival, and credits Bruce Fife's 2008 book on oil pulling therapy with popularising it in the West.[2] The practice then spread through wellness media and celebrity discussion, with the Canadian Dental Association responding in 2014.[1][2] A 2008 article in an Indian dental journal described the therapy for dental audiences.[25] Separately, Wikipedia notes that marketing created a general belief in coconut oil as a healthy food, and that health bodies such as the American Heart Association advise against eating it because of its saturated fat, which concerns consuming the oil rather than swishing it.[23]

Proponents say oil pulling pulls bacteria, plaque and toxins out of the mouth, freshens breath, whitens teeth, soothes gums and supports whole-body health; one review notes the tradition holds it can help with more than thirty systemic conditions.[1][4] Some explanations propose a soap-like, emulsifying action, and an in vitro study examined the mechanism.[18] Wikipedia reports that the detoxification claim has no credible evidence and that no mechanism is understood.[1]

Steven Novella, writing on Science-Based Medicine in 2014, suggested any benefit likely comes from the mechanical act of swishing and that oil pulling is probably less effective than standard mouthwash.[1] The British Dental Journal's 2018 'Bad Science' column also addressed the practice.[17]

On looksmax.org the practice is discussed both as a breath and oral-hygiene habit and as a whitening method. Some posters describe improved breath after a few days, and others describe it as ineffective for whitening and suggest professional whitening or strips instead.[6][7]

Teeth shade and fresh breath contribute to the smile, and community discussion places oil pulling at the low-cost, low-effort end of tooth-care options alongside hydrogen peroxide rinses, strips and dental treatments. Wikipedia's tooth-whitening page notes that mainstream whitening uses hydrogen or carbamide peroxide, which release radicals that break up pigment molecules, a mechanism not shared by oils.[22]

Wikipedia reports that the 2016 systematic review by Gbinigie and colleagues found the included randomized trials few and underpowered, that the American Dental Association states there are no reliable scientific studies supporting oil pulling, and that the Canadian Dental Association said in 2014 it was not convinced of benefits but sensed it would do no harm.[1]

Reviews and meta-analyses of oil pulling and of coconut oil pulling summarise trials on plaque, gingivitis and microbial counts.[4][9][14][15] A 2019 narrative review of coconut oil describes limited but consistent evidence supporting topical use for atopic dermatitis and oil pulling for prevention of dental caries.[9] A reference summary reports that meta-analyses show modest and inconsistent results, with chlorhexidine generally superior for plaque.[2]

Two cases of exogenous lipoid pneumonia associated with repeated sesame oil pulling have been reported in a 66-year-old man and a 38-year-old woman, who habitually pulled oil for several months; diagnosis rested on chest CT ground-glass opacities and lipid-laden alveolar macrophages.[5] A reference summary says the practice is not recommended for children under five because of swallowing risks.[2] Dental authorities describe it as unlikely to cause harm but not a replacement for brushing and flossing.[1]

A randomized, triple-blind trial reported in 2009 compared oil pulling with a control on plaque-induced gingivitis (sesame oil versus chlorhexidine) [10], a 2015 preliminary report studied coconut oil in plaque-related gingivitis [11], and a 2008 triple-blind trial examined Streptococcus mutans counts in plaque and saliva [12]. A 2011 randomized pilot trial studied halitosis and the microorganisms behind it [13].

A 2020 systematic review of coconut oil pulling pooled four randomized trials with 182 participants lasting 7 to 14 days and reported significant reductions in salivary bacterial colony counts and plaque index scores.[8] A 2022 meta-analysis of nine randomized trials found significantly lower salivary bacterial counts in oil pulling groups but no significant difference in plaque or gingival index.[15] A 2024 meta-analysis of 25 trials with 1,184 participants compared oil pulling with chlorhexidine and other mouthwashes on plaque, gingival and bacterial outcomes.[14]

Newer trials include a sunflower oil crossover trial in 26 people with medication-induced dry mouth versus mineral water [16], a four-day plaque regrowth crossover comparison of sesame and coconut oil [20], a sesame oil plaque study published in 2025 [19], and a 2025 trial comparing chlorhexidine, oil pulling and saline for halitosis in orthodontic patients with braces [21]. No clinical trial of tooth whitening was identified.

lore.intro: Oil pulling is discussed on looksmax.org as a low-cost breath and teeth routine, often compared with hydrogen peroxide rinses and professional whitening.[6][7]

claims.believers: Some forum posters say they saw results within days, while another asks whether it works for whitening or only hygiene and others describe no whitening effect.[6][7]
claims.experts: No clinical trial of whitening was identified; trials have studied plaque, gingivitis and microbes.[8][10] Mainstream whitening relies on peroxide chemistry.[22]

claims.claim: Oil pulling improves breath and removes bacteria.
claims.believers: A poster says breath improved and bacteria disappeared.[6]
claims.experts: A randomised pilot trial examined oil pulling for halitosis [13], a 2025 trial compared it with chlorhexidine and saline in braces wearers [21], and a 2016 review found trials small and underpowered.[1]

claims.claim: Oil pulling reduces plaque and gum inflammation.
claims.believers: Practitioners and Ayurvedic reviewers say it lowers plaque and gingivitis.[4]
claims.experts: Randomised trials report reductions in plaque and gingival scores versus controls [10][11], while a 2022 meta-analysis found no significant difference in plaque or gingival index but lower bacterial counts.[15] Chlorhexidine is generally reported to be superior.[2]

claims.believers: Ayurvedic tradition and later promoters say it draws toxins from the body.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports no credible evidence for detoxification claims.[1]

claims.claim: Any benefit comes from soap-like action of the oil.
claims.believers: Some explanations propose that the oil emulsifies bacteria and lowers plaque adhesion, and an in vitro study examined mechanisms.[18]
claims.experts: Novella suggested any benefit is the mechanical effect of swishing.[1]

claims.claim: Coconut oil is the best oil for pulling.
claims.believers: Wellness promoters favor coconut oil, which is about half lauric acid.[23]
claims.experts: A four-day plaque regrowth crossover trial compared sesame and coconut oil [20], and a systematic review pooled four coconut oil trials.[8]

claims.claim: It is a harmless replacement for brushing.
claims.believers: Posters describe it as an easy, cheap addition to oral care.[6]
claims.experts: Dental bodies describe it as unlikely to harm but not supported as a replacement, and two lipoid pneumonia case reports involved aspirated oil.[1][5]
